issues.legal_issue: A rent-control revisional court may reappreciate evidence and interfere with factual findings when the governing revisional jurisdiction permits examination of the legality or correctness of the challenged order.
material_facts: The trial court dismissed the landlord’s eviction petitions after finding that the premises were not required for the landlord’s use or for demolition and reconstruction.
The landlord challenged the dismissals in revision, and the High Court reconsidered the evidence, found the landlord’s requirements established, and ordered eviction.
The tenants argued that the High Court lacked authority to reappreciate the evidence.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s revisional jurisdiction extended to reappreciating evidence and interfering with factual findings, including where the trial court’s finding was entirely improbable; its exercise of that jurisdiction was permissible.
issues.legal_principle: Section 50 of the Karnataka Rent Control Act, 1961 authorizes examination of the legality or correctness of an order and is wider than the revisional power under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Examination of correctness may include reappreciation of evidence and interference with factual findings. The Court relied on Kempaiah v. Lingaiah (2001) 8 SCC 718 and distinguished Phiroze Bamanji Desai v. Chandrakant M. Patel [1974] 3 SCR 267.

predicates.rent_control_revision: A party sought revision of an order made in a rent-control proceeding.
predicates.revision_authorized_examination_of_legal: The governing revisional framework authorized the reviewing court to examine whether the challenged order was legally correct.

issues.definition: When a rent-control order is challenged in revision and the reviewing court is authorized to examine its legality and correctness, the reviewing court may reappreciate evidence and interfere with factual findings.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord may establish a bona fide and reasonable need for personal occupation by seeking to move from an unsuitable existing home to premises intended for residential use.
material_facts: The landlord sought the premises for a residence for himself and his wife, wishing to leave an existing home situated near a drain in surroundings described in the evidence as unhygienic and affected by bad odour.
The tenants’ evidence also acknowledged that the existing home faced a drain and that the landlord did not wish to continue living there.
The landlord had no other premises of his own, and the evidence supported the existence of sufficient reason to move.
The landlord’s family consisted of himself and his wife; the Court held that the absence of children did not defeat the claimed need.
issues.conclusion: The landlord’s need to occupy the premises was bona fide and reasonable; the fact that his family consisted only of himself and his wife did not negate that need.
issues.legal_principle: Section 21(1)(h) of the Karnataka Rent Control Act, 1961 permits recovery where premises are reasonably and bona fide required for occupation by the landlord or a person for whose benefit they are held. The Court held that a landlord’s reasonable wish to leave an unsuitable home may support that requirement and that the tenants cannot defeat a genuine residential choice merely because the landlord has no children. It also relied on the general approach to bona fide requirements discussed in R.V.E. Venkatachala Gounder v. Venkatesha Gupta, AIR 2002 SC 1733, and Harrington House School v. S.M. Ispahani, AIR 2002 SC 2268.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_proceeding and landlord_seeks_personal_residential_occupation and existing_home_is_unsuitable and evidence_supports_the_stated_need

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: A landlord sought eviction of a tenant through a rent-control proceeding.
predicates.landlord_seeks_personal_residential_occu: The landlord intended to occupy the premises as a residence for himself or persons for whose benefit the premises were held.
predicates.existing_home_is_unsuitable: The landlord’s existing home had conditions that gave a reasonable basis for wishing to leave it.
predicates.evidence_supports_the_stated_need: The evidence, including evidence from the tenants, supported the landlord’s stated reason for seeking the premises.

issues.definition: A personal residential need is bona fide and reasonable when, in a rent-control eviction proceeding, the landlord seeks to occupy the premises, the existing home is unsuitable, and the evidence supports the stated need.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord seeking demolition and reconstruction need not prove that the existing building is dilapidated or dangerous, but must establish a bona fide requirement assessed on relevant circumstances.
material_facts: The landlord sought to demolish the old building and construct a residence for his own occupation.
The evidence showed that the building was very old, parts had collapsed, and the tenants acknowledged its age.
The landlord had sufficient financial resources to demolish and reconstruct the building.
The landlord’s proposed use of the reconstructed premises was residential; the Court held that the tenants could not insist that the property be used commercially instead.
issues.conclusion: The landlord established a bona fide and reasonable need for demolition and reconstruction; proof that the building was unfit for human habitation or required immediate demolition was not necessary.
issues.legal_principle: Section 21(1)(j) of the Karnataka Rent Control Act, 1961 permits recovery where premises are reasonably and bona fide required for immediate demolition to erect a new building. The Court applied the principle in Vijay Singh v. Vijayalakshmi Ammal (1996) 6 SCC 475 that a building need not be dilapidated or dangerous, while bona fide intention, the building’s age and condition, and the landlord’s financial capacity are relevant factors. It also relied on R.V.E. Venkatachala Gounder v. Venkatesha Gupta, AIR 2002 SC 1733; A.N. Srinivasa Thevar v. Sundarambal, 1995 (2) Mad LW 14; Harrington House School v. S.M. Ispahani, AIR 2002 SC 2268; and the discussion of P. Orr & Sons in those decisions. The Court emphasized that demolition cannot be permitted merely on the landlord’s assertion, but no fixed age or condition threshold applies.

predicates.rent_control_demolition_and_reconstructi: A landlord sought eviction through a rent-control proceeding on the basis of intended demolition and reconstruction.
predicates.landlord_genuinely_intends_reconstructio: The landlord’s intention to demolish and replace the building was genuine and not merely a device to remove the tenant.
predicates.landlord_can_fund_reconstruction: The landlord had the financial capacity to carry out the proposed demolition and reconstruction.
predicates.relevant_building_circumstances_support_: Circumstances such as the building’s age or condition and the landlord’s proposed use supported the stated need for reconstruction.

issues.definition: A demolition-and-reconstruction requirement is bona fide when the landlord genuinely intends reconstruction, can fund it, and the relevant circumstances support the need, without requiring proof that the building is dangerous or unfit for habitation.

issues.legal_issue: Comparative hardship supports eviction when refusing possession would cause hardship to the landlord and the evidence shows that eviction would not cause hardship to the tenants.
material_facts: The landlord had no other premises of his own and wished to move from a home in an unhygienic location near a drain.
The evidence showed that the tenants would not be put to hardship by eviction from their respective premises.
The High Court considered the circumstances of each tenancy, and the Supreme Court accepted that assessment.
issues.conclusion: The landlord would suffer hardship if unable to move to the premises, while the tenants would not suffer hardship from eviction; comparative hardship therefore did not prevent eviction.
issues.legal_principle: In deciding whether eviction is justified, the court must assess the comparative hardship to the landlord and the tenants on the evidence. The Court applied that assessment to the landlord’s lack of other premises and the evidence that the tenants would not be put to hardship. No earlier case was cited for this issue.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: A landlord sought eviction of tenants through a rent-control proceeding.
predicates.landlord_would_suffer_hardship_without_p: The landlord would face hardship if unable to obtain possession of the premises sought.
predicates.tenants_would_not_suffer_hardship_from_e: The evidence showed that eviction would not cause hardship to the tenants.

issues.definition: Comparative hardship favors eviction when the landlord would suffer hardship without possession and the tenants would not suffer hardship from eviction.
